routes.label: Compare calendars with equal month lengths

officialSolution.label: 2019 AMC 10A

question: Melanie computes the mean \(\mu,\) the median \(M,\) and the modes of the \(365\) values that are the dates in the months of \(2019.\) Thus her data consist of \(12\) copies of \(1,\) \(12\) copies of \(2,\) and so on through \(12\) copies of \(28,\) then \(11\) copies of \(29,\) \(11\) copies of \(30,\) and \(7\) copies of \(31.\) Let \(d\) be the median of the modes. Which of the following statements is true?
solution:
The frequencies let us find the modes and median directly. To compare the mean with them, we can use imaginary calendars whose months all have the same length.

Each number from \(1\) through \(28\) occurs \(12\) times, more often than any other number. These are the \(28\) modes, so their median is
\[
d=\frac{14+15}{2}=14.5.
\]
The median of all \(365\) values is the \(183\)rd value in increasing order. There are \(15\cdot12=180\) values at most \(15\), and \(16\cdot12=192\) values at most \(16\). Thus the \(183\)rd value is \(16\), giving \(M=16\).

If every month had \(28\) days, every number from \(1\) through \(28\) would occur equally often, and the mean would be \((1+28)/2=14.5\). The actual data add some \(29\)s, \(30\)s, and \(31\)s. Since all these added values exceed \(14.5\), we have \(\mu>14.5\).

If every month had \(31\) days, the mean would instead be \((1+31)/2=16\). The actual data result from removing some \(29\)s, \(30\)s, and \(31\)s, all greater than \(16\). Removing these values lowers the mean, so \(\mu<16\).

Therefore \(\boxed{d<\mu<M}\), which is choice \(\boxed{\text{E}}\).
